papers.title: Delta rhythm and voice familiarity organize neural entrainment in the infant brain
papers.abstract: Delta-range rhythms (~0.5-3.5 Hz) are a phylogenetically conserved tempo of biological communication, yet how the infant brain tracks them remains poorly understood. Thirty 6-month-olds heard syllable sequences produced by their mother or a stranger at a delta (2 Hz) or theta (4 Hz) rate, or at irregular intervals, while high-density EEG was recorded. Rhythmic sequences, at both rates, increased low-frequency power over frontotemporal sites. Over frontal sites, only the delta band showed rate-matched tracking: delta-band power was larger for delta-rate than for theta-rate or irregular sequences. This delta-rate-matched response strengthened across blocks. Voice familiarity modulated theta-band power: its increase for delta-rate over irregular sequences was larger for the stranger's voice than the mother's, whereas delta-band tracking was largely insensitive to voice identity. Cortical tracking at 6 months is tuned to the delta rate and shaped by voice familiarity, compatible with an early role of slow rhythms in temporal prediction.

papers.title: An information theoretic approach to evaluating social behaviour in mice using automated home-cage monitoring
papers.abstract: Background: Social behaviour in mice is commonly assessed using standardized assays such as the three-chambered task, which provide controlled measures of sociability but often capture behaviour over short timeframes that may not capture the complex behavioural repertoire exhibited in the home environment. Although automated home-cage monitoring enables continuous, longitudinal assessment of group-housed mice with minimal human interference, methods for quantifying social behaviour in this complex setting remain limited. Information theory offers a framework for measuring statistical dependence between animals but requires one to account for dependence related to the cage environment that arise even in the absence of social interaction. Methods: We developed an information-theoretic approach to quantify social dependence using longitudinal RFID-based positional data from group-housed mice monitored with automated home-cage monitoring system. Mutual information (MI) between cagemates was evaluated against a constrained null model that disrupted within-cage dependence while preserving individual movement patterns. We used two strains with known differences in sociability (C57BL/6J and BTBR) to assess sensitivity to various temporal sampling parameters, test-retest reliability, and correspondence with manually video-scored social behaviours. We further examined variation across genetic backgrounds and investigated relationships between home-cage measures, conventional behavioural assays (three-chamber sociability and open-field behaviour), and brain structure using in vivo MRI. Results: Observed MI was distinguishable from our null distribution, validating its use to quantify statistical dependence beyond that expected from shared cage constraints. MI recapitulated known differences in sociability between C57BL/6J and BTBR mice, showed high test-retest reliability, and correlated with independently video-scored social behaviours. Home-cage social measures also varied across genetic backgrounds and captured strain differences separate from three-chamber sociability. Furthermore, in vivo MRI revealed distinct neuroanatomical patterns for home cage compared to three-chamber sociability measures, including brain regions implicated in social behaviour. Comparisons with open-field measures further indicated that home-cage information-theoretic measures capture behavioural variation not fully represented by conventional measures of locomotion and exploration. Finally, social coordination exhibited distinct temporal dynamics across the circadian cycle. Conclusion: This study establishes and validates an information-theoretic framework for quantifying social dependence from longitudinal home-cage positional data. By accounting for dependence arising from shared environmental constraints and demonstrating reproducibility and correspondence with observed social behaviour, this approach provides a complementary method for characterizing social behaviour in mice. Its application across genetic backgrounds and temporal contexts offers opportunities to investigate behavioural variation beyond the restricted sampling of conventional assays.

papers.title: Sympathetic-to-microglia readouts in human brain single-nucleus data: sparse adrenergic receptor detection and age-associated homeostatic-to-inflammatory shifts in hippocampal microglia
papers.abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) improves sleep in clinical populations, yet the mechanisms linking sympathetic activity to human microglial states remain untested. A prerequisite is to establish what sympathetic signaling readouts exist in human microglia and whether state composition changes in a disease-relevant physiological dimension. Using two public human single-nucleus datasets (the ROSMAP prefrontal cortex resource: 443 donors, 174,420 immune nuclei, 152,459 microglial nuclei, 12 published microglial states; and a hippocampal multiome cohort spanning adult lifespan: 40 donors, ages 20 - 100, 15,225 microglial nuclei), we quantified (i) adrenergic receptor and inflammatory/complement axis gene expression across microglial states, and (ii) donor-level trajectories of four microglial state signatures across age. Adrenergic receptors were barely detected: among nine receptor genes, only ADRB2 was detectable in 3.8 - 11.4% of nuclei, and no adrenergic receptor was state-specific. In contrast, inflammatory genes (nuclear factor-{kappa}B and interleukin modules) were strongly concentrated in one pro-inflammatory state (e.g., NFKB1 mean expression 1.47 vs 0.35 - 0.72 in other states; IL1B in 32.6% of nuclei vs 2 - 16% elsewhere), complement genes in a complement-enriched state, and lipid-metabolism/disease-associated genes in a distinct state. Across the adult lifespan, hippocampal microglia showed a donor-level decline of the homeostatic signature (mean score 0.70 to 0.38 across age quartiles; Spearman {rho} = -0.55, P = 2.6 * 10-4), with concordant rises of pro-inflammatory ({rho} = 0.37, P = 0.017) and disease-associated/lipid-metabolism ({rho} = 0.32, P = 0.045) signatures; an interferon signature showed no age trend. These results (a) indicate that human microglia lack a robust direct adrenergic receptor substrate at single-nucleus resolution, implying that sympathetic influence on microglia, if causal, is likely indirect or low-frequency, and (b) establish a donor-level, age-associated baseline shift toward inflammatory/trimming states in the human hippocampus. Together they define candidate readouts and the baseline against which chronic-sleep-disorder and neuromodulation-intervention studies (e.g., SGB) should be designed.

papers.title: The Dark Side of Light: Adolescent Light Exposure at Night Disrupts Hippocampal Clocks and Plasticity-Related Signaling in a Sex-Dependent Manner.
papers.abstract: In today's society, adolescents are being increasingly exposed to artificial blue light at night from electronic devices, raising concerns about its effects on brain development and mental health. The hippocampus, and specifically the dentate gyrus (DG) regulates memory formation and itself operates as a subordinate circadian oscillator detecting changes in the light environment. However, whether light at night during adolescence can impair hippocampal clock and function remains unknown. To begin exploring this, we exposed adolescent mice to a light cycle disruption (LCD) paradigm consisting of 12hrs of light followed by 5hrs of darkness and 7hrs of blue-enriched light for 5 consecutive days per week, followed by a standard 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness (12L:12D) for 2 days, over a 4-week period. Control animals were maintained under standard 12L:12D. Female and male mice were then tested for novel object recognition (NOR) and novel object location (NOL), and brain tissues were collected for clock gene expression, neuroplasticity markers, and dendritic spine analyses. We found that male mice exposed to LCD spent less time exploring novel objects and locations, and more time with familiar ones, a pattern consistent with impaired recognition and spatial memory, while female mice showed preserved memory performance despite LCD exposure. LCD-exposed male mice showed altered hippocampal daily expression rhythms of Clock and CRY2 levels compared to male control and LCD-exposed females. In addition, we found that LCD-exposed males exhibited reduced p-CREB expression along with reduced Bdnf and dendrite spines numbers in the DG. Interestingly, returning LCD-exposed males to standard 12L:12D conditions for 4 weeks were sufficient to reverse both the behavioral and molecular phenotypes. Together, these results suggest that chronic exposure to light at night during adolescence impairs memory in male mice, through alteration in hippocampal circadian clock regulation and plasticity-related mechanisms within the DG.

papers.title: Neurofeedback enhances a neural signature of selective attention to speech in cocktail-party settings
papers.abstract: Understanding speech in noisy situations is challenging and often fails due to attentional rather than sensory deficits. We report here that neurofeedback can enhance a neural signature of selective attention to speech in a cocktail-party setting. Neural responses to speech were quantified in participants' electroencephalogram (EEG) while they attended to one of two audiobooks, presented simultaneously. After each 22s-segment of speech, the participants' N1 component was extracted from the temporal response function (TRF). The N1 component is known to be sensitive to attention. During a ~49-min training session, N1 amplitude values were displayed visually to participants so that they could learn to strengthen their neural responses to target speech and minimise their responses to distracting speech. During neurofeedback training, we found an enhanced N1 component in the response to target audiobooks that was specific to EEG channels used to provide feedback, and not present in a control group that received sham feedback. At right-lateralised fronto-central channels, enhanced N1 components correlated with improvements in a measure of speech comprehension (multiple-choice content questions). These results indicate that neural responses to speech can be regulated through neurofeedback and open up new possibilities to train attentional listening in populations struggling to understand speech in noise.

papers.title: Development of microsatellite markers with the SSRseq method on Glossina palpalis gambiensis, and G. p. palpalis, and analysis of corresponding field samples from three sleeping sickness foci: Boffa, Dubreka (Guinea), and Bonon (Cote d'Ivoire).
papers.abstract: Tsetse flies are strictly found is sub-Saharan Africa where they are responsible for the transmission and maintenance of African trypanosomiases in humans (HAT) and animals (AAT). Vector control has been recognized as an essential tool to fight against these diseases. Nevertheless, it requires the best possible knowledge of the biology of the targeted population. Population genetics tools can prove very useful to obtain such information but require the use of polymorphic and reliable genetic markers. In this paper we present the development of microsatellite markers using a new high-throughput sequencing based technology (SSRseq). We applied it on two species of tsetse flies from three HAT foci and obtained more accurate results as compared to microsatellite loci developed with classic methods. We could indeed use 9 to 14 SSRseq loci without the several problems generally met with classic microsatellites, as all were located in autosomes, without short allele dominance or stuttering and very few null alleles. SSRseq loci appeared much more polymorphic in tsetse flies as compared to other species (fungi, trees, bees, or fishes), which suggested much higher effective population sizes, much higher mutation rates of the genome or both, suggesting high capacities for evolutionary adaptation. With the 9-14 loci kept, we confirmed the propensity of these flies to move almost freely in the whole zones investigated, and also highlighted the possible evolutionary response of one of the unkept loci regarding vector control devices used in these HAT foci, which will require further studies. We suggest for further population structure studies to use only loci with less than 1% missing data, which proved being a good and fast selection strategy to get the most reliable results.

papers.title: Mapping the invisible: Incidental spatial encoding through haptic exploration
papers.abstract: Active touch provides rich spatial information about object shape. Whether this haptic information can be retained without an explicit memorisation goal remains unclear. Participants explored an unfamiliar two-dimensional raised-dot contour under different sensory conditions and memorisation instructions. Two haptic groups traced the contour hidden from view, either without advance knowledge of the memory tasks (Haptic-Naive) or with explicit memorisation instructions (Haptic-Informed). Reference groups traced the visible contour (Visuo-Haptic-Naive) or viewed it without tracing (Visual-Naive), both without memorisation instructions. Retention was assessed through manual shape reproduction and visual recognition, with a Random-Control group drawing arbitrary shapes as a reproduction baseline. Reproductions in all exploration groups were more similar to the target than arbitrary drawings, supporting incidental spatial encoding in the Haptic-Naive group. Memorisation instructions produced no detectable reproduction advantage but altered exploratory behaviour. Visual feedback improved online tracing without a detectable reproduction advantage over haptic-only exploration. Visual-Naive participants reproduced the shape more accurately than Haptic-Naive participants. Recognition scores were higher following memorisation instructions or exploration with visual information, although Haptic-Naive participants selected alternatives relatively similar to the target. Source-space EEG analyses in the Haptic-Naive group revealed widespread beta-power reductions across bilateral somatosensory, parietal, and occipital regions. Greater reductions in the left lateral occipital complex were associated with more accurate subsequent reproduction. Together, these findings indicate that active touch can support incidental spatial encoding and is associated with changes in cortical activity. The accessibility and use of the retained information are shaped by the goals and sensory context of exploration.

papers.title: Linking Molecular Changes in the Hypothalamus to Alzheimer's Disease Phenotypes
papers.abstract: In many individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD), sleep disruption and weight loss emerge years before the onset of memory decline and dementia. However, the cellular and molecular bases of these early events are not well understood. The hypothalamus is a critical brain region for the regulation of these behaviors, but its response to amyloid has not been systematically characterized. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing to generate transcriptomic profiles of 1.1 million nuclei across the hypothalamus from 10 genetic backgrounds of the AD-BXD genetic reference panel spanning two ages and both sexes, including age-matched controls. Amyloid was associated with widespread, sex-biased molecular changes across diverse cell classes, including elevated neuroinflammatory signatures in microglia and astrocytes, upregulated ion transport pathways across barrier-associated cell types, and sex- and age-dependent changes to primary ciliary pathways in Glp1r+/Lepr+, Histaminergic, and Hcrt+ neuronal populations. Two metabolism-related populations showed differential expression exclusively in one sex: Glp1r+/Lepr+ neurons in females and Gpr50+ neurons in males. Several findings were conserved in analysis of human hypothalamus snRNAseq data, including reduced expression of TGF-{beta} pathway genes in medial mammillary body neurons and increased relative abundance of reactive Serpina3n+/YKL-40 astrocytes. This atlas provides a cellular framework for understanding the early, non-cognitive symptoms of AD and identifies several hypothalamic cell-type specific pathways that represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

papers.title: Joint Representation of Valence and Arousal in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Scenes varying in emotional content are commonly characterized along two affective dimensions: hedonic valence, reflecting pleasantness, and emotional arousal, reflecting intensity. Although prior studies have examined neural representations of valence and arousal separately, it remains unclear how these dimensions are represented jointly and how their representation relates to low-level visual and scene-level properties. Here, we used representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify brain regions whose activity patterns represented the joint valence-arousal structure of affective images and to compare this representation with those of low-level visual and scene-level properties. Twenty participants viewed 60 International Affective Picture System (IAPS) images during simultaneous EEG-fMRI recording. We constructed three image-level representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs): an Emotion RDM derived from valence and arousal ratings; a GIST RDM derived from low-level visual features captured by GIST descriptors; and a Scene RDM derived from CLIP-ViT image embeddings. Searchlight fMRI RSA identified joint valence-arousal representations in lateral occipitotemporal cortex, low-level visual representations in visual cortex, with smaller extensions into right STS and right insula, and scene-level representations across distributed occipital, temporal, parietal, and frontal regions. The valence-arousal representation showed little spatial overlap with the low-level visual representation but was spatially nested within regions representing scene-level properties. EEG-fMRI fusion further indicated that low-level visual representations emerged at approximately 124 ms after stimulus onset, followed by scene-level and valence-arousal representations at approximately 428 ms and 532 ms, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that joint valence-arousal representations are linked to higher-order scene representations, are distinct from low-level visual representations in both space and time, and may support the affective-semantic characterization of visual scenes. Exploratory analyses further showed that valence and arousal ratings generated by multimodal large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) corresponded closely with human ratings and yielded neural representation maps that substantially overlapped with the human valence-arousal map.

papers.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
papers.abstract: We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

papers.title: Sleep EEG distinguishes learned from novel auditory cues without predicting memory retention in a targeted memory reactivation study
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms by which spaced learning promotes understanding
papers.abstract: Spaced learning reliably improves memory. A few studies suggest it also benefits understanding and problem solving, but none has examined the neural mechanism. We hypothesised that this benefit arises because spacing changes the memory trace rather than merely strengthening it. To test this, we taught participants how unfamiliar words meanings could be derived from familiar parts: meaningful rather than rote learning. Each participant learned words in one session, or in two sessions about 2 h (massed) or 48 h (spaced) apart, to the same criterion; one-session words served as the reference. A common interval separated the last session from a delayed test with electroencephalography (EEG). Immediately after learning, self-rated understanding did not differ between schedules, yet under spacing participants revised more of their written test responses between sessions (35% versus 25%). At the delayed test, the spacing effect appeared: recognition was higher and self-rated explanatory retrieval more fluent after spaced than after massed learning. At the neural level, late-retrieval EEG patterns for remembered words were less similar to the reference after spaced than after massed learning, over right frontocentral and temporal sensors. In partly overlapping sensors and windows, lower similarity was statistically associated with a larger fluency advantage, suggesting that the change is directed rather than random. Behavioural evidence hinted at convergence across learners: between sessions, revisions under spacing were smaller and moved responses toward those of others. Together, these findings suggest that spacing changes the memory trace rather than merely strengthening it, in a direction linked to self-rated understanding. Significance StatementSpacing out study helps memory, but any benefit for understanding may not show when study ends. Each learner studied how familiar parts explained unfamiliar words meanings, revisiting some after about two hours and others after about two days. Both schedules ended at the same mastery criterion, with similar ratings of understanding. Yet with the longer gap, learners had revised written explanations more often, in smaller steps toward other learners wording. After an equal delay, they rated those explanations easier to reconstruct. Brain activity during retrieval was consistent with a memory that spacing had reorganised, not merely strengthened, in a way linked to those ratings. The moment a learner feels they understand may be too early to judge a study schedule.

papers.title: The emergence and neural organisation of facial-expression information during ultra-brief vision
papers.abstract: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.
